sources.publisher: Better Health Channel, Victorian Department of Health

read: Fridge temperature 5 °C or below; check it with a thermometer.
Freezer temperature below -15 °C.
Danger zone 5 °C to 60 °C; keep high-risk food at 5 °C or below, or above 60 °C.
Cool hot food in shallow dishes or smaller portions; wait until steam stops rising before refrigerating.
Keep defrosted food in the fridge until cooking; cook straight away if defrosted in a microwave; never refreeze raw food after thawing.
High-risk food left in the danger zone for more than 4 hours should be thrown out.
If unsure of the use-by date, throw it out.
Cooked rice and eggs listed as high-risk foods.

sources.title: Food safety when cooking
sources.publisher: Better Health Channel, Victorian Department of Health
sources.licence: © State of Victoria. No open licence stated; Better Health terms of use apply (https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/about/terms-of-use). Facts restated in our own words, linked to the source.
read: Cook food to at least 75 °C; use a thermometer.
Keep hot food hotter than 60 °C.
Cool food once steam stops rising, then cover and refrigerate; shallow trays or smaller portions cool faster.
Cooked food keeps a few days in the fridge in ideal conditions; to keep it longer, freeze it once cooled in the fridge.
Danger zone 5 °C to 60 °C, high-risk food: up to 2 hours reheat, refrigerate or eat; over 2 hours and under 4 hours eat immediately; more than 4 hours throw out.
Reheat to above 75 °C or preferably until boiling, with steam coming through the whole food, not just the edges.
Raw-egg foods such as homemade mayonnaise, hollandaise, tiramisu and mousse need extra care; do not give them to pregnant women, young children, elderly people or anyone with a chronic illness.
Store raw meat and poultry at the bottom of the fridge, apart from cooked food.

sources.title: Food use-by and best-before dates
sources.publisher: Better Health Channel, Victorian Department of Health
sources.licence: © State of Victoria. No open licence stated; Better Health terms of use apply (https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/about/terms-of-use). Facts restated in our own words, linked to the source.
read: Food with a use-by date must be consumed before or on that date; do not eat it after, even if it looks and smells fine.
Best-before is about quality, not a strict safety cutoff; food that looks and smells as expected should generally be safe after the date.
Storage and packaging affect how long food lasts.

sources.title: Food safety and eggs
sources.publisher: Better Health Channel, Victorian Department of Health
sources.licence: © State of Victoria. No open licence stated; Better Health terms of use apply (https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/about/terms-of-use). Facts restated in our own words, linked to the source.
read: Keep eggs in their carton in the fridge; the best-before date assumes the fridge.
Throw out dirty or cracked eggs; do not wash eggs.
Cook eggs and egg foods until hot all the way through.
Homemade foods with raw or lightly cooked egg (mayonnaise, aioli, hollandaise, mousse, custard, tiramisu, uncooked batter or dough) are often linked to food poisoning.
Symptoms are often more severe in pregnant women, older people and people with chronic illness.

sources.title: Food poisoning - prevention
sources.publisher: Better Health Channel, Victorian Department of Health
sources.licence: © State of Victoria. No open licence stated; Better Health terms of use apply (https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/about/terms-of-use). Facts restated in our own words, linked to the source.
read: Avoid food past its use-by date and food in swollen, dented, leaking or damaged packaging.
See your doctor as soon as possible if you think you have food poisoning.
Nurse-On-Call 1300 606 024, 24 hours, 7 days.
Report illness to your local council or the Department of Health, especially if it may be linked to a restaurant, cafe, shop or takeaway.

read: Keep perishable food at 5 °C or colder.
Danger zone 5 to 60 °C.
Left at room temperature: under 2 hours return to the fridge; 2 to 4 hours eat straight away; after 4 hours throw away.
Do not thaw frozen food at room temperature; thaw in the fridge or use a microwave.
Do not eat food past its use-by date.

lines.text: Set the fridge to 5 °C or colder, and use a fridge thermometer to check it.
The freezer should be colder than -15 °C.
Germs grow fastest between 5 °C and 60 °C. Keep food that spoils easily below that range or above it.
Keep raw meat on the bottom shelf, away from cooked food.
A use-by date is about safety. Do not eat the food after that day, even if it looks and smells fine.
A best-before date is about quality. Food that looks and smells as it should is generally fine to eat after it.
If you are not sure about a use-by date, throw the food out.
Let the steam stop rising, then cover the food and put it in the fridge. Shallow dishes or smaller portions cool faster.
Cooked food keeps a few days in the fridge. To keep it longer, freeze it once it has cooled in the fridge.
Reheat until it is steaming all the way through, above 75 °C, or until it boils. A thermometer helps.
Cooked rice is on Victoria's list of foods that spoil easily, so the same leftover steps apply: cool it, cover it and refrigerate it soon after it is cooked.
The pages we read give no timings that are just for rice, so none are given here.
Keep eggs in their carton in the fridge. Do not wash them.
Throw out eggs that are cracked or dirty.
Cook eggs until the food is hot all the way through.

Homemade foods with raw or lightly cooked egg, such as mayonnaise, hollandaise, mousse and tiramisu, are often linked to food poisoning. Pregnant women, young children, older people and anyone with a long-term illness are advised not to eat them.
Thaw frozen food in the fridge or in a microwave, not on the bench.
Keep thawed food in the fridge until you cook it. If you thawed it in a microwave, cook it straight away.
Do not freeze raw food again once it has thawed.
Food that spoils easily and has sat between 5 °C and 60 °C for under 2 hours can go back in the fridge, be reheated or be eaten.
After 2 hours and up to 4 hours, eat it straight away.
After 4 hours, throw it out.
Also throw out food past its use-by date, cracked or dirty eggs, and food in packaging that is swollen, dented, leaking or damaged.
If you think you have food poisoning, see your doctor as soon as you can.
For a food complaint, or to report an illness you think came from a restaurant, cafe, shop or takeaway, contact your local council. The Department of Health also takes reports.

notFound: Victorian leftovers page (betterhealth.vic.gov.au food-safety-leftovers) returned 404; the cooking and storage pages were used instead.
No official page read gives a number of days for leftovers in the fridge, only 'a few days', so no number is shown.
No official page read gives rice-specific cooling, storage or reheating timings. The FSANZ Bacillus cereus PDF could not be read as text, so nothing from it is used.
The Department of Health 'Your guide to food safety' PDF could not be extracted as text, so nothing from it is used.
Fridge wording differs between Better Health pages ('5 °C or below' on storage, 'below 5 °C' on prevention); the storage page and FSANZ ('5 °C or colder') agree and are used.

1300 364 352 appears as the 'Food Safety Hotline' on Better Health and as the recall line on the Safe Food Victoria page; the labels differ, so the number is not shown. The Safe Food Victoria complaint page is linked instead.
No official consumer page read gives a cold-water thawing method for home use (the Department's FoodSmart page says it is not recommended), so it is not covered.
Pregnancy, weakened immune system and Listeria advice is not covered here; it needs its own page and review.

The Department of Health food-complaint page (health.vic.gov.au/food-safety/making-a-complaint...) redirects to Safe Food Victoria; councils' own complaint pages were not read, so no council phone number is given.
